inside_knee.title: Inside a Healthy Knee
points: Smooth cartilage covers the bone ends so the knee glides.
Ligaments and tendons hold the knee steady.
Cartilage has no nerves, so pain comes from other parts.
explain: Cartilage gives a smooth, low-friction surface; it has no blood vessels and no pain-sensing nerves.
The synovium lines the joint and makes fluid that lubricates and nourishes the cartilage.
Bone under the cartilage, menisci, ligaments, tendons, muscles, nerves and vessels work together as one system.
options: Education and self-management about how the joint works
Strengthening for quadriceps, hamstrings and hip muscles
Weight management when relevant, to reduce joint load
ask: Where exactly is the pain, and what makes it worse?
Is there swelling, warmth, or stiffness after rest?
What has your joint problem stopped you from doing?
refer: Hot, swollen, painful joint with fever: urgent evaluation for infection.
Inability to bear weight, deformity, or sudden loss of function after injury.
A genuinely locked knee: evaluate for a treatable mechanical obstruction.

whole_joint.title: Arthritis Is a Whole-Joint Disease
points: Arthritis is more than “wear and tear.”
Cartilage, bone, the joint lining, and other parts can change.
Two people with similar X-rays can hurt very differently.
explain: OA involves cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, menisci, ligaments and surrounding tissues, not cartilage alone.
Pain can come from inflamed synovium, subchondral bone, the joint capsule, periarticular tissues and sensitized nerves.
Similar X-rays can hide different biology: some patients have more synovitis, others more structural or bone changes.
options: Education, exercise and physical therapy as the foundation
Weight management, bracing or a cane when appropriate
Topical or oral NSAIDs, weighing each patient’s risks
Injections or GAE if symptoms persist despite good care
ask: How long does morning stiffness last?
Are other joints swollen or painful?
How is the pain affecting your sleep and activity?
refer: Persistent swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, or symmetric small-joint involvement: consider inflammatory arthritis and rheumatology.
Hot, swollen joint with systemic symptoms: urgent evaluation for septic arthritis.

referred.title: Where Pain Starts Isn’t Always Where It Hurts
points: Hip or back problems can cause pain felt in the knee.
Finding the true source helps pick the right treatment.
Tell us about numbness, tingling, or pain in other areas.
explain: Hip disease and lumbar spine problems can produce pain felt around the knee, thigh or buttock.
Knee-directed treatment may not help if the main pain source is elsewhere.
GAE treats pain arising from the knee itself; it cannot fix pain coming from the hip or spine.
options: Treat each pain generator on its own terms
Knee treatments, including GAE, when the knee is the main source
Separate evaluation and care for hip or back pain
ask: Does the pain spread into your thigh, buttock or lower back?
Do you have numbness, tingling or weakness?
Are several joints affected, or have you had fever?
refer: Back pain with new bladder or bowel dysfunction or saddle numbness: emergency.
New weakness, numbness, limb color or temperature change, or absent pulses.
Persistent swelling of small hand or foot joints: rheumatologic evaluation.
referred.alt: Three body outlines showing pain that starts in the neck and is felt in the shoulder or arm, starts in the lower back and is felt in the buttock, thigh or knee, and starts in the hip and is felt in the groin, thigh or knee

kl_grades.title: How Knee Arthritis Is Graded
points: Doctors grade knee arthritis on an X-ray from 0 to 4.
Higher grades mean more changes in the joint’s shape.
Your grade does not measure how much you hurt.
explain: Kellgren–Lawrence grades radiographic OA 0 to 4: none, doubtful, definite but mild, moderate, severe.
The grade reflects osteophytes, joint-space narrowing, sclerosis and deformity — it is not a measure of pain.
Some patients have major structural change with little pain; others have significant pain with milder X-ray findings.
options: Knee X-ray as the first imaging test
MRI when X-rays are nondiagnostic or specific problems suspected
Plan treatment on symptoms, function and imaging together
GAE typically considered for mild-to-moderate OA; some advanced cases too
ask: Does your X-ray match how your knee feels day to day?
What activities has your knee pain stopped you from doing?
refer: Grade 4 with major deformity: orthopedic assessment — do not delay it solely to pursue GAE.
Severe pain with only mild X-ray changes: look for other pain sources (hip, spine, meniscus).
kl_grades.alt: Five knee drawings showing Kellgren-Lawrence grades 0 to IV, with the joint space narrowing and bone spurs growing from grade to grade

spectrum.title: Your Treatment Options, From Self-Care to Surgery
points: Exercise and self-care are the base of every plan.
Shots or GAE may help if pain keeps going.
Surgery is an option when joint damage is advanced.
explain: Education, exercise, physical therapy and weight management are core OA care, not just a waiting period.
Steroid injections give short-term relief for some; evidence for hyaluronic acid and PRP is mixed.
GAE and replacement are not interchangeable; replacement suits advanced structural disease when nonsurgical care has failed.
options: Exercise, PT, weight management, bracing, topical or oral NSAIDs
Steroid injection for short-term relief; HA and PRP evidence mixed
GAE for persistent knee OA pain in selected patients
Osteotomy, partial or total knee replacement when indicated
ask: What would you do if your knee hurt less?
Which treatments have you tried, for how long, and did they help?
Are you hoping to avoid or delay surgery?
refer: Advanced OA with substantial pain and functional loss despite nonsurgical care: orthopedic assessment.
Persistent symptomatic knee OA despite appropriate care: GAE consultation.
Features of inflammatory arthritis: rheumatology.
spectrum.alt: Treatment options for knee osteoarthritis in three groups: medicines and injections, GAE, and surgical options from osteotomy to total knee replacement, all built on an ongoing foundation of education, exercise and weight management

lining.title: Inside the Joint Lining: Extra Vessels and Nerves
points: Arthritis can make the thin lining inside the knee swollen.
New blood vessels and nerves can grow there and add pain.
GAE aims to calm these extra vessels, not fix cartilage.
explain: Inflamed synovium signals new vessel growth; new vessels may let in more inflammatory cells, sustaining a cycle.
Sensory nerves may grow alongside new vessels, and inflammation can make nerve endings more sensitive.
This is one possible contributor to OA pain; mechanisms remain under investigation and sham-controlled trials are mixed.
options: Foundation care: exercise, physical therapy, appropriate medications
Steroid injection to reduce inflammation short term
GAE to reduce flow to selected abnormal vessels
ask: Does your knee swell or feel warm?
Where is your single most painful spot?
Is the pain worse at night or at rest?
refer: Persistent symptomatic knee OA despite appropriate care: discuss GAE evaluation.
Suspected rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis: rheumatology — GAE is not an established first-line treatment.
lining.alt: A healthy, thin joint lining beside an inflamed, thickened lining with more blood vessels, sensory nerve fibers and inflammatory cells

gae_vs_tkr.title: GAE and Knee Replacement Are Different Tools
points: GAE treats painful blood vessels through a pinhole in an artery.
Knee replacement swaps damaged joint surfaces using open surgery.
GAE does not rebuild cartilage or straighten a crooked knee.
explain: GAE targets abnormal vessels feeding inflamed tissue; replacement removes and replaces damaged joint surfaces.
GAE: local anesthesia, usually home same day, routine activity within days. Replacement: weeks to months of rehabilitation.
Having GAE does not prevent a later replacement, but it is not a substitute when surgery is clearly indicated.
options: GAE: persistent pain, not ready for or unsuited to surgery
Total knee replacement: advanced structural damage and deformity
Partial replacement or osteotomy for one-compartment disease
ask: What worries you most about surgery?
Has an orthopedic surgeon evaluated your knee?
What result would make a treatment worthwhile for you?
refer: Major deformity or advanced disease where replacement is indicated: do not delay orthopedic consultation.
Persistent OA pain in a patient wishing to delay or avoid surgery: GAE consultation.

candidate.title: Is GAE Right for Me?
points: Good fit: knee arthritis pain despite 3+ months of good care.
Pain from your hip, back, or nerves needs a closer look.
An infection or a tear needing surgery usually rules it out.
explain: Often a good fit: OA knee pain of 5/10 or more limiting daily life despite 3+ months of good conservative care.
Typically mild-to-moderate OA on X-ray; some advanced cases with active synovitis may still benefit.
Patients must understand GAE reduces symptoms, does not reverse OA, and benefit may be limited or fade.
options: Optimize exercise, PT, weight and medications first
GAE for selected persistent symptomatic knee OA
Orthopedic assessment for major deformity or structural failure
Coverage varies; many insurers consider GAE investigational
ask: How long have you had pain, and how bad is it from 0 to 10?
What treatments have you tried, and for how long?
Do you take blood thinners, or have kidney disease or a contrast allergy?
refer: Usually not a fit: active infection, advanced PAD, meniscus or ligament tear needing surgery, major malalignment.
Inflammatory arthritis as the main cause of pain: rheumatology.
Mild PAD, kidney disease, contrast allergy or bleeding risk: needs careful evaluation, not automatic exclusion.

gae_day.title: A Typical GAE Day
points: Most people go home the same day.
A numbing shot is used, and many people stay awake.
The procedure itself often takes about one to two hours.
explain: Local anesthetic at the access site, often the groin; some centers add IV sedation. Many patients stay awake.
Angiography shows abnormal “blush”; a microcatheter delivers embolic material to selected branches while sparing normal tissue.
The procedure commonly takes about one to two hours; most patients go home the same day after observation.
options: Bring a complete list of medicines and supplements
Don’t stop medicines unless your specialist says so
Follow fasting instructions; arrange a driver if sedated
ask: Do you take blood thinners, antiplatelets or diabetes medicines?
Do you have kidney problems or a contrast dye allergy?
Who can drive you home?
refer: Anticoagulation: coordinate a periprocedural plan with the prescribing physician.
Access-site bleeding, uncontrolled pain or other concerns: longer observation or admission.
gae_day.alt: Six steps of a typical GAE day: check-in, preparation, the GAE procedure (often about 1 to 2 hours), recovery, discharge review, and going home

recovery.title: The Road to Recovery After GAE
points: Expect a sore knee for a few days.
Pain may ease over weeks; we review progress at 3–6 months.
Keep exercising — it helps you get the most from GAE.
explain: First week: knee ache or flare, access-site bruising, possible skin color change; routine activity within days.
Pain often starts easing in weeks 2–6; most benefit by 3–6 months, tracked with KOOS or WOMAC.
Results vary; some get years of relief, others less. Studies without a sham group likely overstate the effect.
options: Resume and progress physical therapy as pain eases
If pain returns: reassess, repeat GAE, or other treatments
Orthopedic evaluation if structural disease progresses
ask: How far can you walk now compared with before?
Are you keeping up with your exercises?
Has the pain changed location or character?
refer: Returning pain: rule out a new meniscal tear or hip or back source first.
Repeat GAE: expert consensus suggests waiting at least three months on the same knee.
Structural progression with disability: orthopedics — prior GAE does not prevent replacement.
recovery.alt: Recovery timeline after GAE: day 0 initial recovery, days 1 to 7 early recovery, weeks 2 to 6 assess early response, months 3 to 6 review progress, and 6 months and beyond continue knee care

after_call.title: After GAE: What’s Normal and When to Call
points: A mild ache, small bruise, or tiredness is normal.
Call for fever, new swelling, worse pain, or skin changes.
Cold, numb leg or heavy bleeding? Call 911.
explain: Skin discoloration happens when embolic material reaches tiny skin vessels; it usually fades over days to weeks.
Small skin ulcers occasionally occur and usually heal on their own with monitoring.
At the access site, a small bruise is common; a firm, growing or very painful swelling is not.
options: Pain relief as recommended by the care team
Monitor and treat any skin breakdown
Prompt evaluation of access-site swelling or bleeding
ask: Any fever, chills, or spreading redness or warmth?
Is your foot cold, pale, blue or numb?
Is the skin over the knee blistering or darkening?
refer: Cold, numb leg or heavy bleeding: call 911.
Severe or rapidly worsening knee pain not controlled by recommended relief.
Numbness or tingling in the foot or leg that does not go away.
after_call.alt: Three columns of symptoms after GAE: often mild and temporary, call your care team now, and call 911 now, plus what to do for puncture-site bleeding

beyond.title: Embolization Beyond the Knee
points: The same idea is being tried in the shoulder, elbow, and heel.
Research is early, mostly small studies, and results vary.
Regular care comes first; this is for pain that won’t improve.
explain: Frozen shoulder, tennis elbow, plantar fasciitis, hip and hand OA: evidence is mostly small case series without controls.
After knee replacement, embolization has an established role for recurrent bleeding; data for persistent pain are early.
Consider only after a confirmed diagnosis and several months of standard care; results are uncertain.
options: Frozen shoulder: physical therapy, injections, time
Tennis elbow: activity modification, physical therapy, time
Plantar fasciitis: stretching, footwear, orthotics, physical therapy
Embolization for selected patients not improving with standard care
ask: How long has the pain lasted despite treatment?
Has imaging ruled out a tear, fracture or nerve compression?
Do you understand the evidence is still early?
refer: Sudden pop with weakness pushing off: prompt assessment for Achilles rupture.
Pain after knee replacement: exclude infection, loosening and instability first.
Recurrent bleeding into a replaced knee: embolization evaluation.
